intro/hello: This lecture is about mixtures of experts: how to give a model far more parameters without making each token any more expensive.
intro/dense: In a dense transformer, every parameter works on every token.
intro/price: So the size of a model and its price are welded together: double the parameters, and every token costs twice as much.
intro/ffn: Two thirds of each block sits in one place: the feed-forward network, or F F N, which works on each token alone.
intro/copies: A mixture of experts makes many copies of that block, called experts, each with its own weights.
intro/router: And it adds a tiny router, which looks at each token and picks just a few experts to run.
intro/active: The layer now holds eight times the parameters, but each token pays for only two of the eight.
intro/mixtral: Mixtral eight by seven B, for example, stores about forty seven billion parameters, and runs about thirteen billion for each token.
intro/catch: The catch is sharing. Left alone, a router sends almost everything to a few favorite experts.
intro/plan: So after the layer itself, the story is about balance: a loss, fixed buffers, smarter experts, and bias terms. And then, how experts spread across many G P Us.
layer/token: Follow one token through the layer. It arrives as a vector, x, of d numbers.
layer/logits: The router is a single matrix, W r, with one column per expert. Multiplying by it gives one score per expert: the logits.
layer/softmax: A softmax turns those scores into probabilities, p, that add up to one.
layer/topk: Then top k: keep the k largest, here two, and drop the rest. The dropped experts never run for this token.
layer/gates: The two kept probabilities become the gates, g: how much each chosen expert counts.
layer/run: Only the two chosen experts run. Each one is an ordinary feed-forward block, with its own weights.
layer/sum: Their outputs are added up, each one weighted by its gate.
layer/residual: And the result joins the residual stream, exactly where a dense F F N output would go.
layer/cost: So the compute depends on k, not on E. Add more experts, and each token still costs the same.
layer/every: G shard replaced every other feed-forward layer this way. Mixtral replaces all of them.
router/classifier: Look closer at the router. It is the linear classifier from the start of C S two thirty one N, with experts in place of classes.
router/arrows: Each column of W r is an arrow in token space. A token's logit for an expert is how well it lines up with that arrow.
router/regions: So the router carves the space into regions, one per expert, with straight borders.
router/probs: This token lands between experts one and zero: probabilities of zero point three seven and zero point three two, and small ones for the rest.
router/topk: Keep the top two. Their probabilities add up to only zero point seven.
router/renorm: Many designs renormalize: divide by that sum, and the gates become zero point five four and zero point four six, adding up to one.
router/same: That is exactly a softmax over the kept logits alone, which is how Mixtral writes its router.
router/switch: Not every design does this. With top one, a renormalized gate would always be exactly one, and the router would get no signal from the task.
router/switch2: So the Switch Transformer keeps the raw probability, and scales the chosen expert's output by it.
router/learn: Nobody labels which expert a token should use. The router learns only through its gates: if a bigger gate would have lowered the loss, the border moves.
params/two: An expert model has two parameter counts, and both of them matter.
params/total: Total parameters are everything stored: every expert in every layer. They set the memory, and the room for knowledge.
params/active: Active parameters are the ones a token actually runs through: the shared parts, plus k experts per layer. They set the compute.
params/name: Take Mixtral eight by seven B. The name suggests eight times seven, or fifty six billion.
params/shared: But only the feed-forward blocks are copied. Attention and the embeddings are shared: about one point six billion parameters.
params/expert: Each expert is three matrices, four thousand by fourteen thousand: a hundred and seventy six million numbers, in each of thirty two layers.
params/sum: Eight experts per layer gives forty six point seven billion in total. Two per token gives twelve point nine billion active.
params/price: So Mixtral needs the memory of a forty seven billion parameter model, and spends the compute of a thirteen billion one.
params/sixnd: In the scaling law's six N D, the N is the active count.
params/batch: One warning. A single token reads two experts per layer, but a batch of sixteen tokens touches nearly all eight.
params/memory: So every expert must sit in memory, and with big batches, every one of them is read at every step.
collapse/free: So far, the router may do whatever it likes. Two things go wrong.
collapse/hardware: First, hardware. Experts usually live on different G P Us, and if one expert gets half the batch, its G P U works while the others wait.
collapse/pace: The whole layer runs at the speed of its busiest expert.
collapse/feeds: Second, and worse, imbalance feeds itself. An expert that gets more tokens gets more gradient, so it improves faster...
collapse/more: and the router, which learns to prefer whatever lowers the loss, sends it even more.
collapse/toy: Here is a real run: two hundred and forty tokens of two numbers each, four linear experts, and a top one router.
collapse/task: Each token carries a target, shaped like a square funnel with four flat faces. One linear expert can fit only one face.
collapse/start: The tokens share an offset, the way real token vectors share directions. So from the start, blue wins most of them.
collapse/run: Train with no balancing. Blue takes the rest. The other three experts receive nothing, and never learn.
collapse/collapse: That is expert collapse. One expert does all the work, and the model has paid for parameters it never uses.
collapse/shazeer: Shazeer and his colleagues described exactly this self-reinforcing loop in twenty seventeen.
auxloss/fix: The fix that made experts practical is a small extra loss, lowest when the load is even.
auxloss/f: For each expert, measure f i: the share of the batch's tokens actually sent to it.
auxloss/P: And capital P i: the average probability the router gave it, over the same tokens.
auxloss/loss: The Switch Transformer multiplies the two, adds them up over the experts, and multiplies by E, the number of experts.
auxloss/one: When the load is even, every f and every P is one over E, and the loss is exactly one.
auxloss/E: When every token goes to one expert with full confidence, the loss is E: four, here.
auxloss/grad: Why two factors? The share f comes from an argmax, a count. Nudge the router a little, and no count changes, so f has no gradient.
auxloss/P2: P is a smooth average of softmax outputs, so it does. The loss uses f as a weight, and moves P.
auxloss/push: The gradient on each P is proportional to its f, so the busiest expert's probability is pushed down hardest.
auxloss/alpha: A small coefficient, alpha, zero point zero one in the Switch paper, keeps balance from outweighing the task.
balance/resume: Back to the collapsed run. Keep the weights exactly as they are, and switch the loss on.
balance/borders: The router's borders start to move. Tokens at the edge of blue's region are pushed toward the idle experts.
balance/train: Now those experts receive tokens, so at last they get gradient, and they start to fit their part of the funnel.
balance/quarter: Within a few hundred steps, every expert has about a quarter of the tokens.
balance/faces: And the regions line up with the four faces of the target.
balance/better: The task loss falls by a factor of about twenty. Balance was not only for the hardware: it is what put the idle parameters to work.
balance/weak: Too small an alpha, like zero point zero zero one in this toy, is not enough to pull the router out.
balance/zloss: Two more habits came later. S T M o E added a router z loss: a small penalty on large router logits, which keeps training stable.
balance/precision: And routers are usually computed in full thirty two bit precision, even when the rest of the model runs in B F sixteen.
capacity/shapes: Accelerators like arrays whose shapes are known in advance.
capacity/buffer: So the classic implementation gives each expert a buffer of fixed size, its capacity, C, before it sees the batch.
capacity/factor: C is the even share, k times T over E, times a capacity factor: say, one point two five.
capacity/line: Tokens claim slots in arrival order. A running count down the batch gives each token its place in its expert's line.
capacity/full: A token whose expert is already full is dropped.
capacity/residual: It skips the experts entirely, and passes to the next layer unchanged, through the residual connection.
capacity/fluct: Even with perfectly fair odds, random fluctuations overfill some buffer at a factor of one.
capacity/tradeoff: Raise the factor and the drops vanish, but every empty slot is compute and memory reserved for nothing.
capacity/skew: And with a skewed router, no reasonable factor saves you. Balance has to come first.
capacity/dropless: Later systems stopped dropping. Mega blocks handles any number of tokens per expert with block sparse kernels, and DeepSeek V three reports dropping no tokens at all.
deepseek/what: DeepSeek M o E, in twenty twenty four, asked what an expert should be.
deepseek/big: With sixteen big experts and top two routing, each expert covers a lot of ground, so common knowledge gets copied into several of them.
deepseek/split: The first change: split every expert into four narrower ones, and route each token to four times as many.
deepseek/same: The parameters stay the same, and so does the compute per token.
deepseek/combos: But the number of possible teams explodes: from a hundred and twenty ways to pick two experts out of sixteen...
deepseek/billions: to over four billion ways to pick eight out of sixty four.
deepseek/special: With that many combinations, each expert can afford to specialize narrowly.
deepseek/shared: The second change: shared experts. A few experts run on every token, with no routing at all.
deepseek/why: They hold what every token needs, so the routed experts need not each relearn it. Each token is routed to one fewer expert, so the compute stays fixed.
deepseek/v3: DeepSeek V three uses one shared expert and two hundred and fifty six routed ones, eight per token: six hundred and seventy one billion parameters in total, thirty seven billion active.
bias/compromise: An auxiliary loss is a compromise. Its gradient lands in the same weights as the task's, and a strong one can cost some quality.
bias/v3: DeepSeek V three balances without a loss.
bias/bias: Each expert gets a bias, b, that is added to its score only when choosing the top k.
bias/weigh: The gates still use the unbiased score, and no gradient ever reaches the biases.
bias/update: After every step, an overloaded expert's bias goes down by a small fixed amount, gamma, and an underloaded expert's bias goes up.
bias/price: It works like a price. A popular expert gets slightly more expensive, so tokens near its border move to a neighbor.
bias/toy: Here is the collapsed toy again, with alpha at zero, and the biases switched on.
bias/even: The idle experts' biases climb, and the load evens out, without touching the task gradient.
bias/safety: DeepSeek V three still keeps a tiny balance loss as a safety net, but the biases do the work.
parallel/big: A model with hundreds of billions of parameters does not fit on one G P U.
parallel/ep: Expert parallelism is the natural split: put different experts on different G P Us. Here, four of them, with two experts each.
parallel/tokens: Each G P U runs attention on its own slice of the batch. At an expert layer, the router picks a destination for every token.
parallel/dispatch: Then comes an all to all: every G P U sends a different packet to every other one, so each token lands where its expert lives.
parallel/compute: The experts run on whatever arrived.
parallel/combine: A second all to all sends each result back home, where it is scaled by its gate and added to the residual stream.
parallel/traffic: That is two trips per token per layer, each carrying its full vector: for four thousand tokens at Mixtral's width, about a hundred megabytes per G P U, per layer.
parallel/skew: And here balance shows up in the hardware. If two popular experts sit on one G P U, it receives twice its share...
parallel/wait: and since no one can start the next layer until the combine finishes, everyone waits for it.
parallel/limits: Systems overlap this traffic with computation, and limit how far a token may travel: DeepSeek V three sends each token to at most four machines.
outro/layer: To sum up. A mixture of experts swaps one feed-forward block for many, and a router runs only the top k for each token.
outro/counts: Total parameters set the memory. Active parameters set the compute.
outro/collapse: Left alone, routing collapses onto favorites. The Switch loss, E times the sum of f times P, is one when balanced, and pushes the busiest experts down.
outro/capacity: Fixed buffers drop the overflow onto the residual stream. Dropless kernels and good balance avoid it.
outro/deepseek: DeepSeek M o E uses many small experts plus shared ones, and DeepSeek V three balances with bias terms instead of a loss.
outro/a2a: And expert parallelism moves tokens with two all to alls per layer, at the pace of the busiest G P U.
outro/idea: Underneath it all is one idea: how much a model knows, and how much each token costs, no longer have to grow together.
outro/end: Store a lot, run a little, and keep the load even.
